newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Oil prices cut Kuwait deficit, but reform needed.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices cut Kuwait deficit, but reform needed.

text.p: Kuwait needs to apply fundamental economic reform to balance its books instead of relying on oil price rises to bridge its budget gap, economists said on Sunday.
"It is crucial to avoid the impact of any steep fall in oil prices," said one. "We simply cannot afford to have a big budget deficit."

The deficit of the tiny Gulf Arab state, which runs one of the world's most lavish welfare states, has been eating chunks of its nest egg of overseas reserves, the source of funds used to pay the bills for its 1991 liberation war against Iraq.
"Whenever oil prices rise, deficit pressure eases and enthusiasm to apply reform fades," said leading economist Jassem al-Saadoun. Furthermore, "We start to increase spending."
"A fall in oil prices creates pressure for borrowing and we start hearing talk about economic reform," Saadoun said.
Higher-than-expected oil prices helped Kuwait to slash to 653 million dinars ($2.2 billion) a projected 1.32 billion dinar deficit in the 1995/96 fiscal year which ended in June.
Economists expect oil prices for the remainder of 1996 to remain well above the $13 a barrel projected in the budget. Oil accounts for 85 percent of the desert state's export earnings.

Parliament in October passed a 4.2 billion dinar budget for fiscal 1996/97 with a forecast net deficit of 1.2 billion dinars based on the same estimate for oil prices. For most of the past two years the price for Kuwait's crude has been $15 or higher.
The firm oil prices have helped Kuwait raise GDP at current prices 8.2 percent to 7.95 billion dinars in 1995. Inflation this year is privately estimated at about three percent.

But National Bank of Kuwait, the country's largest commercial bank, has said: "It would be quite risky if the current fortuitous drop in the deficit were to give the government a false sense of comfort and reduce the sense of urgency for introducing structural changes."

Planning officials have said the oil-rich state should consider raising revenue by introducing tax on Kuwaiti firms, hiking petrol prices, imposing duties on luxuries, cutting subsidies on public utilities and pursuing privatisation.
Saadoun suggests cuts in military spending and large state projects. "The most important move is to cut spending; specifically that related to defence and big projects."
Many Kuwaitis say they will never accept paying tax, or even higher electricity, water or telephone bills as long as they see the government lavishing cash on non-productive projects.
"High oil prices have the effect of an aspirin on most Gulf states," said a diplomat. "They prefer it to surgery."
